summary: Identifies the information that implementers of email and MIME header field generators and parsers need about each field. When specifications leave this out, implementers have to guess and interoperability can suffer. The memo lists what a good field specification should say. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If every toy came without instructions, people would guess how to play and argue. This memo tells the toy makers which instructions to include.

subtitle: Guide for writing clear email header field specifications.

tldr.problem: When email and MIME header field specifications are incomplete, implementers have to guess, leading to interoperability failures.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4249 identifies what information every header field specification needs to include: syntax rules, field properties, semantics, and considerations for compatibility and security.
tldr.outcome: Implementers have a checklist for writing clear field specifications, reducing ambiguity and incompatible implementations.

facts.label: Naming rules covered
facts.value: Content-, Resent-, Accept-, List-, and others

today: RFC 4249 remains the informational guide for email header field specifications and has not been obsoleted, so it continues to serve as reference material for specification authors.

sections.title: Why Header Field Specifications Matter
sections.content:
Internet message headers and MIME-part headers consist of fields with names and content. While the Message Format (RFC 822) and MIME specifications (RFCs 2045 and 2046) define some fields, they also allow extension fields created by implementers.

When a specification for a new field is vague or incomplete, implementers make different assumptions about how it should work. This leads to incompatibility. RFC 4249 is not a technical standard itself, but an informational guide that identifies what a good field specification must explain.
sections.eli5: Every email has headers that say who sent it and what it is. Sometimes new header types are added, and if the rules are unclear, different programs will handle them differently.

sections.title: Established Conventions and Naming
sections.content:
Header fields follow certain naming patterns and terminology. Several naming rules are formally defined in RFCs:

  • Fields with the Content- prefix must be used only for MIME extension fields.
  • Fields with the Resent- prefix follow specific rules for resubmitted messages.

Additionally, conventions have developed for other prefixes: Accept- for content negotiation fields, List- for mailing list information, Original- for references to related messages, and others. A good specification should indicate which naming pattern applies and be consistent with these conventions.
sections.eli5: Email headers follow a naming code. Some start with Content- (for message parts), others with List- (for mailing lists), and so on. A good spec says which pattern it uses.

sections.title: Specification Checklist
sections.content:
A complete field specification should include several items:

  • ABNF syntax: A formal grammar that clearly specifies where whitespace, comments, and line folding are allowed or forbidden, using existing ABNF productions from RFC 2822.
  • Field instances: The minimum and maximum number of times the field may appear in a single header.
  • Categorization: What type of field it is (e.g., trace field, address field), which affects how intermediaries handle it.
  • Semantics: Who may generate the field, who may modify it, and who should interpret it.
  • Context: Which headers (message header or MIME-part header) the field may appear in.
  • Security: Potential security implications.

The specification should also address backward compatibility and how the field interacts with existing mechanisms.
sections.eli5: A good field specification needs to say: what it looks like (the format), how many times it can appear, who writes it, who reads it, and any safety concerns.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Legacy Content
sections.content:
A large installed base of email applications exists. Many change slowly or not at all. When a new field or syntax extension is introduced, older implementations may not recognize it. A specification must carefully consider what older implementations will do:

  • They might simply ignore the field, which is fine if that is the intended behavior.
  • They might misinterpret the field and behave unexpectedly.
  • They might break when encountering unfamiliar syntax.

Additionally, email is often archived and accessed long afterward. New extensions should not change the meaning of messages that lack them. A field specification must be explicit about these compatibility concerns.
sections.eli5: Old email programs still exist and won't know about new header types. A spec needs to say whether it is okay for them to ignore it, and whether a message without the header means something different.

sections.title: Security, Internationalization, and IANA
sections.content:
Every field specification should include a Security Considerations section that explains potential risks. Some fields carry sensitive information; others may affect how intermediaries process messages.

If the field contains human-readable text in multiple languages, the specification must address internationalization, typically using the mechanism in RFC 2047 as amended by RFC 2231. If the field defines protocol keywords that might be extended in the future, these should be registered with IANA via a registry, with clear procedures for adding new keywords. Specification authors should coordinate with IANA well before publication.
sections.eli5: A header spec needs to say: what could go wrong if someone misuses it, whether it needs to work in other languages, and whether new keywords might be added later.
